title: Concurrency Practices & Smells
body:
# Concurrency Practices & Code Smells

## Never block the executor

```rust
// BAD inside async fn
std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2));   // stalls every task on this worker

// GOOD
let _ = tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2)).await;
// CPU-heavy work?
tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || crunch(numbers)).await??;
```

Rule: async contexts only await; blocking goes to `spawn_blocking` or threads.

## Bound everything you spawn

```rust
// BAD: unbounded per-request spawn → OOM under load
for conn in incoming { tokio::spawn(handle(conn)); }

// GOOD: semaphore/queue caps concurrency
let permits = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(64));
```

Unbounded task creation is the async equivalent of a fork bomb.

## Careless `.await` ordering

Awaits run sequentially unless joined. Two independent fetches awaited back-
to-back double latency — `tokio::join!(a, b)` runs them concurrently while
keeping structured cancellation.

## Unnecessary shared mutable state

Every `Arc<Mutex<…>>` is a coordination cost. Prefer channels passing owned
messages; share read-only data (`Arc<Config>`); isolate writes behind one
task owning the resource.

## Structured cancellation

Long-running tasks should select on a shutdown signal (`tokio::select!`) so
cancel propagates cleanly instead of leaking tasks that outlive their UI.
This app's execution registry is the reference implementation.
